# 02 From Neighbours to Latent Structure {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## 🎰 Bandit Time: Which statement best describes a latent factor? {background-color="#003D7C"}

<div class="bandit-options">
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#D32F2F"><strong>A.</strong> An item attribute recorded directly by the platform.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#1976D2"><strong>B.</strong> An inferred interaction pattern represented by a learned embedding coordinate.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#388E3C"><strong>C.</strong> A verified demographic fact about a user.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#7B1FA2"><strong>D.</strong> A manually fixed value shared by every user.</div>
</div>

::: notes
:::

## Sparse Neighbourhoods Can Fall Silent

<div class="matrix-grid">
  <div class="matrix-head"></div><div class="matrix-head">Item A</div><div class="matrix-head">Item B</div><div class="matrix-head">Item C</div><div class="matrix-head">Item D</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">User 1</div><div class="matrix-rated">5</div><div class="matrix-rated">4</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">User 2</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-rated">5</div><div class="matrix-rated">4</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">User 3</div><div class="matrix-rated">4</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-rated">5</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">Target user</div><div class="matrix-rated">5</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-target">?</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div>
</div>


::: notes
Ask students to identify the Week 01 bottleneck: few co-rated items can make a local similarity estimate unstable or unavailable. Do not claim that factorisation removes missingness.
:::

## Global Patterns Remain in the Matrix

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Neighbourhood CF

- Starts with local overlap.
- Compares named rows or columns.
- Can be silent when overlap is thin.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Latent-factor model

- Learns shared coordinates from many interactions.
- Uses global patterns to score a user–item pair.
- Still inherits the limits of its evidence.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip .to-think-about title="To think about"}
Does a learned representation make a missing interaction more trustworthy—or only make a prediction possible?
:::

::: notes
The intended answer: it makes a prediction possible by exploiting patterns elsewhere; it does not convert a missing observation into ground truth.
:::

## Factorisation Learns Shared Coordinates

$$
R \approx P Q^\top
$$

<div class="factor-flow">
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Interaction matrix \(R\)</strong><br>Observed user–item feedback with many blanks.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">≈</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>User matrix \(P\)</strong><br>One learned vector per user.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">×</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Item matrix \(Q\)</strong><br>One learned vector per item.</div>
</div>

A small number of learned coordinates can capture recurring interaction patterns more compactly than the full sparse matrix.

::: notes
Introduce factorisation intuitively first. \(P\) and \(Q\) are parameter matrices; individual dimensions are useful for scoring even when they do not have a stable human-readable name.
[Sources]
- Koren, Y., Bell, R., & Volinsky, C. (2009). Matrix factorization techniques for recommender systems. *Computer*, 42(8), 30–37.
:::

## Factors Are Patterns, Not Personal Facts

| Tempting shortcut | Better statement |
|---|---|
| “Dimension 3 is this user’s identity.” | Dimension 3 is a learned coordinate associated with interaction patterns. |
| “The factor is a hidden genre tag.” | A factor may correlate with metadata, but it is inferred rather than recorded. |
| “The factor explains the person.” | The factor helps the model score candidates under particular data and objectives. |

::: notes
This slide sets the language discipline for the rest of the lecture. Do not reify embeddings as psychological or demographic truth.
:::

## A Dot Product Turns Embeddings into a Score

$$
\hat r_{ui} = p_u^\top q_i
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### User vector

$$p_u=[p_{u1},p_{u2},\ldots,p_{uk}]$$

Captures a learned location in the model’s coordinate system.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Item vector

$$q_i=[q_{i1},q_{i2},\ldots,q_{ik}]$$

Captures how the item aligns with those learned patterns.
:::
:::

The dot product is high when the vectors align along dimensions the model has learned to reward.

::: notes
Make the transition from visual alignment to the compact scoring rule. A score is not the entire recommendation policy: it may later be filtered, re-ranked, or evaluated differently.
:::

## Worked Calculation: Two Items, One Current Score

$$
p_u=[0.8,0.2], \qquad q_A=[0.9,0.1], \qquad q_B=[0.4,0.8]
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Item A

$$
\hat r_{uA}=0.8(0.9)+0.2(0.1)=\mathbf{0.74}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Item B

$$
\hat r_{uB}=0.8(0.4)+0.2(0.8)=\mathbf{0.48}
$$
:::
:::

**Current model verdict:** Item A is higher scoring.

**Still unresolved:** diversity, constraints, exposure, uncertainty, and the rest of the candidate list.

::: notes
This is the required worked calculation. Ask students to verify each product before revealing the totals. State clearly that this is a score comparison, not a complete ranking policy.
:::

## Training Adjusts Both Sides of the Match

<div class="factor-flow">
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Observed interaction</strong><br>User watches, clicks, rates, or purchases.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Model score</strong><br>Apply \(p_u^\top q_i\).</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Loss and update</strong><br>Move both user and item vectors.</div>
</div>

- **Explicit feedback:** a rating can support a prediction-error loss.
- **Implicit feedback:** a positive interaction can be compared against sampled alternatives.
- Repeated updates create embeddings that reflect the selected learning signal.

::: notes
Connect the loss to the type of evidence, not simply to an implementation preference. This prepares the contrast between rating prediction and ranking.
:::

## Regularisation Limits Convenient Stories

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{P,Q}\; \mathcal{L}
&= \sum_{(u,i)\in\Omega}(r_{ui}-p_u^\top q_i)^2 \\
&\quad + \lambda\left(\lVert P\rVert_F^2+\lVert Q\rVert_F^2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

- The first term fits observed interactions.
- The regularisation term discourages overly flexible parameter values.
- The design question is not “fit or regularise”; it is how to generalise beyond the interactions already seen.

::: notes
Explain the two terms qualitatively. \(\lambda\) controls a trade-off and should not be treated as a universal constant.
[Sources]
- Koren, Y., Bell, R., & Volinsky, C. (2009). Matrix factorization techniques for recommender systems. *Computer*, 42(8), 30–37.
:::

## Worked RecBole Example: BPR on MovieLens 100K

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
<div class="code-panel"><pre style="margin:0;color:inherit;"># test.yaml
USER_ID_FIELD: user_id
ITEM_ID_FIELD: item_id
load_col:
  inter: [user_id, item_id]
embedding_size: 64
epochs: 500
metrics: ['Recall', 'MRR', 'NDCG']
topk: 10

# run.py
from recbole.quick_start import run_recbole
run_recbole(model='BPR', dataset='ml-100k',
            config_file_list=['test.yaml'])</pre></div>
:::
::: {.column width="39%"}
### What is happening?

- **BPR** is a matrix-factorisation model trained pairwise for personalised ranking.
- RecBole loads user–item interaction columns, learns user/item embeddings, and evaluates a ranked list.
- `embedding_size` selects the dimension of both learned vectors.
:::
:::

::: notes
This is the required worked RecBole example. Present it as a compact, reproducible configuration—not a live installation task. The official quick start uses BPR with `ml-100k`, interaction columns, 64-dimensional embeddings, and ranking metrics including Recall, MRR, and NDCG.
[Sources]
- RecBole documentation, “Quick Start: General Recommendation.” https://recbole.io/docs/get_started/started/general.html
- RecBole documentation, “BPR.” https://recbole.io/docs/user_guide/model/general/bpr.html
:::

## Read the RecBole Output as a Design Claim

| Output artefact | What it can support | What it cannot establish alone |
|---|---|---|
| Training loss | Whether the stated loss changes during optimisation. | Real-world user value or fairness. |
| Recall@10 / NDCG@10 | A ranking comparison under the declared held-out protocol. | A production outcome without further evaluation. |
| Top-*k* candidates | A concrete prompt for inspection and error analysis. | A causal explanation of a user’s preference. |
| Learned embeddings | A representation used by the model. | A human identity or a verified metadata field. |

::: notes
Ask: “What would you inspect before making a claim about this model?” Expected answers include split protocol, held-out metric, candidate set, examples of failures, and the source of interaction data.
[Sources]
- RecBole documentation, “Quick Start: General Recommendation.” https://recbole.io/docs/get_started/started/general.html
:::

# 03 Objectives, Continuity, Novelty, and Consequences {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## Prediction Rewards Accurate Numbers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Question

How close is \(\hat r_{ui}\) to an observed rating or score?
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Typical evidence

An explicit rating, a known score, or another numeric target.
:::
:::

A prediction objective is useful when a numeric estimate itself drives a decision. Error measures such as RMSE summarise how close estimates are to observed values.

::: notes
Do not say that RMSE is always the right metric. It is aligned with a prediction target, not necessarily with a top-k recommendation experience.
:::

## Ranking Rewards Useful Order

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Question

Do useful items appear above less useful alternatives in the visible list?
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Typical evidence

Implicit interactions, held-out positives, and candidate ordering.
:::
:::

Ranking measures, such as **NDCG@10**, reward useful items placed nearer the top of a displayed list.

::: notes
Make the positional idea concrete: a user cannot benefit much from a relevant item buried well below the visible top-k.
:::

## 🎰 Bandit Time: What should the home screen optimise? {background-color="#003D7C"}

<p class="bandit-question"><strong>A home screen must order ten candidate items for immediate display.</strong> Which measure most directly tests whether useful items appear near the top?</p>

<div class="bandit-options">
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#D32F2F"><strong>A.</strong> RMSE over predicted ratings.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#1976D2"><strong>B.</strong> NDCG@10.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#388E3C"><strong>C.</strong> The number of metadata tags per item.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#7B1FA2"><strong>D.</strong> The age of the user account.</div>
</div>

<p style="margin-top:.7em;color:#80cbc4;font-size:.73em;">Answer: <strong style="color:#ffffff;">B</strong>. NDCG@10 is position-sensitive; it tests the ordering of useful candidates in the displayed top-*k*.</p>

::: notes
This is MCQ 2 of 2. Invite a quick comparison with A: RMSE is meaningful for a numeric prediction task but does not directly assess top-k order.
:::

## 👥 Activity 1: Choose an Objective, Then Defend It {background-color="#003D7C"}

<p class="activity-question"><strong>Work in pairs.</strong> Choose one case. Write a single line: <em>task → objective → metric → one assumption</em>.</p>

<div class="activity-grid">
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>Restaurant rating</h3>Predict a score after a meal. What is the target? What would count as a close estimate?</div>
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>Personalised feed</h3>Order a visible list now. What does “near the top” mean?</div>
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>Job retrieval</h3>Surface plausible jobs from a large candidate set. Whose relevance definition is being used?</div>
</div>

<div class="activity-output"><strong>Produce:</strong> one defensible objective/metric pair and one assumption you would want to test. Be ready to compare it with a pair using a different case.</div>

::: notes
This is student activity 1 of 2. Give pairs time to formulate the line; take two contrasting examples and point out that an objective is a product decision with distributional consequences.
:::

## ♠ Spades: Stable Preferences Need More Than One Tag

- A loyal, metadata-oriented user may return to durable interests: familiar creators, formats, categories, or constraints.
- One static tag is too coarse: it misses interaction history, combinations of features, and changing context.
- A latent-factor model can represent stable patterns, while metadata helps make an explanation or constraint legible.

::: {.callout-tip .to-think-about title="To think about"}
How could a system preserve continuity without treating last year’s interaction history as a permanent identity?
:::

::: notes
Introduce the Spades treatment as a situational design lens, not a fixed kind of person. It should guide the case study’s continuity question.
:::

## ♠ Observed Metadata Meets Learned Continuity

| Layer | What it contains | Appropriate use |
|---|---|---|
| **Observed metadata** | Creator, category, format, duration, or an explicit constraint. | Interpretability, filtering, feature-based comparison. |
| **Latent embedding** | Inferred coordinates from interaction patterns. | Candidate scoring and learned associations. |
| **Case design** | A deliberate combination of both. | Preserve meaningful continuity while monitoring drift and blind spots. |

**Guardrail:** *latent metadata* is a teaching bridge for the case—not a claim that an embedding coordinate is a recorded field.

::: notes
State the guardrail explicitly. Students can use this distinction in E1: explain how metadata and a latent model might jointly serve a surface without conflating them.
:::

## ♦ Diamonds: Novelty Should Be Relevant, Not Random

- Feature-based novelty identifies candidates that differ in meaningful, declared attributes from the familiar set.
- The objective is not surprise for its own sake; it is a credible opportunity for discovery.
- A novelty mechanism needs a definition of difference, an exposure policy, and an evaluation consequence.

::: notes
Make Diamonds distinct from Spades: Diamonds foreground diversity, long-tail exposure, and discovery; they should not be presented as a generic preference for “more random” items.
:::

## ♠ + ♦ Re-rank With a Familiar Anchor

<div class="factor-flow">
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Latent score</strong><br>Generate plausible candidates from interaction patterns.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Spades anchor</strong><br>Keep credible continuity for the user’s stable context.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Diamonds re-rank</strong><br>Reserve selected positions for feature-different discovery.</div>
</div>

Possible checks: top-*k* relevance, feature coverage, long-tail exposure, repeat engagement, and who is not receiving discovery.

::: notes
This is the core case-study design pattern. Ask students which control belongs in the model objective and which can appear in a downstream re-ranking rule. Both can be legitimate, but the rationale and evaluation must be explicit.
:::

## 📶 AI Voice Mode: Whose Discovery Is Missing? {background-color="#003D7C"}

<div class="voice-prompt">
<strong>Live prompt for the voice agent</strong><br><br>
A recommender’s interaction logs are dominated by popular titles. Independent and long-tail items had far less initial exposure, so they have fewer observed interactions. The system adds feature-based novelty for some users. Explain why low interaction may not mean low preference; identify one risk if exposure history is treated as preference; and propose one measurement that could test whether the novelty mechanism broadens meaningful discovery rather than merely lowering relevance.
</div>

<p style="margin-top:.65em;color:#ffffff;font-size:.72em;"><strong>Listen for:</strong> assumptions about exposure, missing stakeholders, and a measurable distinction between opportunity and preference.</p>

::: notes
This is the required ethics voice-agent example. The title follows the course AI Voice Mode convention. The agent is a conversation partner, not an authority: pause to distinguish supported reasoning, assumptions, omissions, and claims requiring evidence.
:::

## 👥 Activity 2: Audit the Agent’s Explanation {background-color="#003D7C"}

<p class="activity-question"><strong>Small groups.</strong> Audit the voice-agent response instead of accepting its fluency.</p>

<div class="activity-grid">
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>One assumption</h3>What did the agent assume about interaction logs, users, or items?</div>
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>One omission</h3>Which stakeholder or under-exposed group could be harmed or overlooked?</div>
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>One measurement</h3>What observable quantity would help separate exposure from preference?</div>
</div>

<div class="activity-output"><strong>Produce:</strong> one three-part audit. Be ready to state why the proposed measurement changes the design decision.</div>

::: notes
This is student activity 2 of 2. Collect two groups’ audits. Emphasise that an apparently convincing explanation is not evidence; the instructor remains responsible for accuracy and synthesis after the AI interaction.
:::

## 🔑 <u>Historical Behaviour Becomes Model Geometry</u> {background-color="#003D7C"}

| Historical process | Model consequence | Design question |
|---|---|---|
| Uneven exposure | Sparse or distorted interaction evidence | Who had a genuine chance to interact? |
| Popularity reinforcement | Well-exposed items gain stronger learned signals | Who receives repeated visibility? |
| Feature-based novelty | A re-ranking decision changes what becomes observable next | Who receives credible discovery—and who does not? |

<p style="margin-top:.85em;color:#EF7C00;font-weight:bold;">🤞 Use history as evidence with limits, not as a neutral record of preference.</p>

::: notes
Use this navy key-point slide to close the ethics section. Tie together objective, representation, exposure, and the difference between continuity and lock-in.
:::

# 04 From Model to Case Study {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## From Interaction Data to a Ranked Candidate List

<div class="factor-flow">
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Collect & inspect</strong><br>Understand feedback, missingness, and exposure.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Learn & score</strong><br>Train embeddings under an explicit objective.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Re-rank & evaluate</strong><br>Apply continuity, novelty, and responsible checks.</div>
</div>

A production recommender is a chain of technical and product decisions—not just a latent-factor score.

::: notes
This is the conceptual implementation laboratory. Avoid presenting it as a complete production architecture; it provides the chain students can narrow for E1.
:::

## E1 Bridge: Choose the Consequential Decision

For one approved recommendation surface, make a focused argument around a choice such as:

| Choice | Example question |
|---|---|
| Representation | Why use an embedding-based model rather than only local neighbourhood evidence? |
| Objective | Why should the surface optimise top-*k* order rather than numeric prediction? |
| Continuity | How should observed metadata and learned preferences support a Spades-oriented need? |
| Novelty | Which feature-based difference should create Diamonds-style discovery, and how will it be evaluated? |
| Risk | How could historical exposure bias distort the evidence used by the model? |

::: notes
Invite students to select one or two rows that could form a coherent argument. Do not encourage a catalogue of every possible model component.
[Sources]
- CP4285 Essay 1 brief, `static/essays/e1.md`.
:::

## 🔑 <u>Representation Enables; Objectives and Constraints Decide</u> {background-color="#003D7C"}

- **Latent factors** make distributed interaction patterns usable when local overlap is weak.
- **Objectives** decide what the model is rewarded for predicting or ranking.
- **Spades and Diamonds** make continuity and discovery explicit design choices.
- **Ethical scrutiny** asks how past exposure shaped the evidence in the first place.

<p style="margin-top:.8em;color:#EF7C00;font-weight:bold;">🔑 A better score is not automatically a better recommendation.</p>

::: notes
This key-point slide is the end-of-lecture synthesis before the pre-lecture task and final summary.
:::

# Summary {background-color="#003D7C"}

## 🔑 <u>Latent Factors Learn Structure; Responsible Systems Learn Limits</u>

| Week 01: neighbourhood CF | Week 02: latent-factor models |
|---|---|
| Uses observed local overlap | Learns global user/item representations |
| Similarity is specified directly | Representation is learned from interaction patterns |
| Thin overlap can make neighbours unreliable | Distributed patterns can support a score—but not create ground truth |
| Main question: who counts as a neighbour? | Main questions: what is optimised, who receives continuity or novelty, and how did history shape the evidence? |
